metadata.title: Predicting adolescents’ environmental action: From individual to national-level factors using an explainable machine learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018, which is implemented as a two-stage stratified probability-proportional-to-size design with schools sampled first and then a random set of up to 42 students selected within each school. The authors report PISA response-rate targets at the school (85%, weighted) and student (80%, weighted) levels and note that systems failing to meet these thresholds were excluded from the public database, supporting national representativeness within participating systems. However, the manuscript does not state whether PISA sampling weights (or any replicate weights) were applied in the machine-learning training/evaluation pipeline. Because the models are standard ML classifiers (LightGBM, XGBoost, Random Forest, MLP) and the paper does not describe weight-aware training, the safest interpretation is that complex survey weights were not explicitly incorporated; this may leave some clustering/unequal selection effects only partially addressed by the PISA design rather than by analysis weights.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables are private- and public-sphere environmental action outcomes derived from PISA 2018 questionnaire items rather than PV-based cognitive achievement scores. Missing data handling is reported: the study imputes missing values using predictive mean matching via the MICE package, and it also addresses class imbalance using SMOTE. Therefore, no PV- or missing-data reporting gap is present for the modeled outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2018 dataset and restricted the analytic sample to adolescents who answered the environmental-action items; after excluding students who did not respond to these items, the final sample comprised 420,339 adolescents from 66 countries. The study does not report additional grade-level restrictions beyond the PISA target population (15-year-olds) and does not describe further exclusions (e.g., missing predictors) beyond the imputation step. For modeling, the dataset was split into training (90%) and testing (10%) sets, with stratified 10-fold cross-validation applied within the training set.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Model selection: LightGBM best for public-sphere; XGBoost selected for private-sphere. Validation (Table S6): XGBoost highest accuracy 0.830, recall 0.830, AUC 0.709; Random Forest highest F1 0.780 (vs 0.768 for LightGBM). Test (Table S7): XGBoost highest accuracy and recall (both 0.833) with AUC 0.718; Random Forest slightly higher F1 0.781 (vs 0.772).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged environmental attitude, critical thinking, climate-change explanatory capacity, international event discussion, and school collaboration atmosphere to predict private-sphere environmental actions, finding that XGBoost achieved the highest accuracy/recall (test accuracy 0.833; test recall 0.833; test AUC 0.718) with strong generalization from validation to test. This indicates that strengthening individual competencies and school-supported learning processes may improve adolescents’ household/private pro-environmental behaviors, though the cross-sectional design prevents causal direction claims.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Validation (Table S4): LightGBM highest accuracy 0.699, F1 0.698, recall 0.699; AUC 0.762. Test (Table S5): LightGBM best with accuracy 0.700, F1 0.702, recall 0.702; AUC 0.767. Consistency between validation and test indicates good generalization.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 the study leveraged environmental attitude, school belonging, World Governance Index (WGI), mean Sustainable Development Score, and climate risk index (CRI) to predict public-sphere environmental actions, finding that LightGBM achieved the best performance (test accuracy 0.700; test F1 0.702; test recall 0.702; test AUC 0.767) with consistent validation-to-test results. This indicates that public pro-environmental participation is jointly shaped by individual attitudes, school socialization, and national context, suggesting that education policy should pair classroom/school belonging initiatives with national sustainability messaging and governance signals, while recognizing that SHAP-based importance is not causal evidence.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 (15-year-olds) to predict two types of adolescent environmental action—private-sphere and public-sphere—using explainable machine learning. After excluding adolescents who did not answer the environmental-action items, the final sample includes 420,339 students from 66 countries. For public-sphere actions, LightGBM was best, reaching test accuracy 0.700, F1 0.702, recall 0.702, and AUC 0.767; for private-sphere actions, XGBoost was selected based on highest accuracy/recall (test accuracy 0.833, recall 0.833, AUC 0.718), with Random Forest slightly higher F1. Missing values were imputed using predictive mean matching (MICE), and class imbalance was addressed with SMOTE. The paper uses SHAP for feature contribution and reports nonlinear patterns, but the cross-sectional design and lack of explicit survey-weight incorporation mean results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects.
